extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers and students (computer science / cognitive science) interested in heuristic search, problem solving methods, and Polya-style auxiliary-problem techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation criteria for using auxiliary problems in heuristic problem solving and for designing AI problem-solving systems (problem-space representations, heuristics, and mechanisms for finding/using auxiliary problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem solver's capabilities expressed by problem spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem solver's basic capabilities are expressed by the problem spaces it can employ. It is able to work on any problem in a space; problems outside this space lie outside the problem solver's competence or even comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design/assess a solver by the set (union) of problem spaces it supports; if a target problem is outside those spaces, the solver cannot be expected to handle it. Consider competence as the union of spaces the solver can employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic search (definition and cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic search = the combinatorial search that arises whenever there is uncertainty in the application of an operator; the combinatorial character of search follows inevitably from the cascading of uncertain applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or building systems, recognize that uncertainty in operator application produces search effort; heuristics are knowledge used to modulate this combinatorial search as much as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-space components (states, operators, start/goal, heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem space should be specified by its states (e.g., expressions, partial layouts, plans), operators (e.g., theorems, moves, refinements), an initial state, a goal state, and heuristic knowledge about operators/states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling a task, explicitly define these components. Heuristic knowledge must be brought to bear via mechanisms for selecting/rejecting operators and states, evaluation functions, models, planning, etc. Examples: GEOMETRY THEORIST (states = geometric figures; operators = theorems), SAINT (states = algebraic expressions; operators = integration rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-centered problem space
rubrics_metrics.description: Object-centered problem space: A problem space whose states are generated from the objects in the problem by structural composition operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that object-centered spaces (states = object-structures) limit certain kinds of creativity: e.g., they represent expressions rather than proofs, losing ability to start from an imperfect/wrong proof and transform it into a correct one. For tasks requiring auxiliary problems or manipulations across problem-statements, object-centered representations may be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-centered problem space
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem-centered problem space: A problem space whose states are generated from problem statements (constraints, conditions) rather than just structural decomposition of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer or consider problem-centered representations when the task requires manipulating constraints, generating auxiliary problems, or representing problems (not just objects) as primary entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to bring heuristics to bear
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic mechanisms include selection and rejection of operators and states, evaluation functions, models, causality analysis, planning, construction of macro-objects, and hierarchy/plan abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems by which of these mechanisms they implement; combine mechanisms to make search 'intelligent' and to exploit domain knowledge effectively (examples: selection/rejection mechanisms in SAINT; causality analysis and macro-objects in DESIGN PROBLEM SOLVER).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's techniques for finding auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of heuristic prompts to find auxiliary problems: (1) Have you seen the problem before? (2) Have you seen the problem in a different form? (3) Do you know a familiar problem with the same unknown? (4) Do you know a familiar problem with a similar unknown? (5) Here is a related problem and solved before. Could you use it? Its result? Its methods? (6) Solve first some related problem. (7) Do you know a more accessible related general problem? (8) Do you know a more special problem? (9) Do you know an analogous problem? (10) Use the data somehow! i.e., create a problem using the same data. (11) Solve the problem keeping only part of the condition. (12) Restate the problem. Restate it still differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these prompts as retrieval cues or generative heuristics when searching for auxiliary problems. Note: many of these are retrieval-oriented (memory/oracle based) rather than constructive; some (e.g., drop a condition, restate) are more directly usable in programmatic generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary-problem method (three stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The auxiliary-problem method comprises three stages: (1) find an auxiliary problem, (2) solve the auxiliary problem (recursive problem solving), (3) use the auxiliary problem (use result, method, or attempt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing solvers, treat the middle stage as standard recursion but give special attention to the first and third stages: finding and using auxiliary problems are nontrivial and often under-specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to use an auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's taxonomy for using a solved auxiliary problem: (1) use the result; (2) use the method; (3) use the attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which of these three modes is applicable. 'Using the attempt' typically arises after failure of the first two and is a salvage operation leading to new auxiliary problems. Systems should be evaluated on their ability to apply all three uses (particularly interpreting methods and reusing partial attempts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wild vs tame subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Wild subproblem: A subproblem whose use in the main problem is still a problem even after it is solved. Tame subproblem: A subproblem that is not wild; how to use it is already known when it is generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether generated subproblems are tame (predictably usable) or wild (require additional 'connection' problem solving). The thesis: current AI lacks capability to handle wild subproblems; designing for wild subproblems demands explicit mechanisms to connect solved auxiliaries to main problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection problem (connecting auxiliary result to main problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection problem: How to connect the solved auxiliary problem with the main problem. It is itself a distinct subproblem that takes two problems as given and asks how one might be related to the other in terms of its solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using an auxiliary problem, explicitly consider and formulate the connection problem as a subgoal; solving it often requires fresh acts of problem solving and cannot be assumed automatic. Systems should provide mechanisms (search, analogy, plan interpretation) to pose and solve connection problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of stages / factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: There is virtually complete independence between (finding), (solving), and (using) the auxiliary problem; what is done with an auxiliary problem once solved need bear no relation to how it was found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design/assessment should treat each stage separately and provide interfaces/mechanisms to bridge them (e.g., mapping of representations, retrieval cues, plan interpreters) because properties of generation do not constrain how a solution can be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan interpretation and analogical mapping when using methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an auxiliary problem as a method requires plan-interpretation machinery: take a step in the plan and set up a subgoal of finding the analog step in the main problem. Systems like NOAH and MOLGEN implement such machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems on their plan-interpretation capability and analogical mapping. Using a method (plan) yields a pre-determined connection structure (less wild) but still requires robust analog-finding and step-matching mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory retrieval and use of long-term experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's view: auxiliary problems are often found in the problem solver's prior experience (long-term memory); retrieval cues depend on where attention is focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide plenty of retrieval cues and content-addressable memory mechanisms when designing systems that rely on recalling auxiliary problems; recognize that many auxiliary-problem generations are retrieval, not constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint management and causality analysis (design problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics for spatial/design problems include preserving uncluttered space, fitting larger objects first, handling the greater difficulty and irreversibility of constraint failure; use causality analysis to assign causes for failures and backtrack far enough, and construct macro-objects that weld together interrelated constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For layout/design domains, evaluate solvers on their ability to manage constraints, identify causal sources of failures (enabling independency-directed backtracking), and package tightly-related components into macro-operators to reduce search complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independency-directed backtracking (EL example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independency-directed backtracking: when a contradiction is generated (a failure of a particular type of constraint), remove only those constraints that have caused the difficulty because constraints can be known to be independent of the difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor backtracking methods that exploit independence among constraints to avoid unnecessary undoing of unrelated work; evaluate systems for the ability to track causal dependencies among constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of abstract plans and plan-space search (NOAH/MOLGEN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create hierarchies of abstract plans specifying incomplete sequences of actions; work in the space of plans where operators expand plans to additional levels of detail and rearrange plans to remove redundancies, avoid conflicts and coordinate actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tackling sequential/spatial tasks, prefer plan-space representations with abstraction hierarchies and operators that refine plans; evaluate solvers for plan-expansion, conflict-avoidance, and plan-rearrangement capabilities.
